questions.title: Does an officer’s statement that he “needs to come inside” turn a consent into acquiescence to authority under Bumper?
questions.question_body: In this case, the officer said, “I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure [the kids are okay],” after the wife had initially said she’d prefer the police not enter. The court says, in context, that wasn’t coercive and cites Hicks. But in Bumper v. North Carolina, consent is invalid if it’s simply acquiescence to a claim of lawful authority. Where is the line between an urgent, safety-framed request (“we need to”) and a claim of authority that vitiates consent? How much do courts weigh tone, prior refusals, and the brevity of the exchange when deciding whether the word “need” crosses into coercion?

questions.title: Did Georgia v. Randolph require police to obtain the co-occupant’s consent when the husband was inside but silent?
questions.question_body: The husband (defendant) was in a back bedroom when the wife consented at the doorway. The opinion doesn’t discuss Randolph, which bars reliance on one occupant’s consent when a physically present co-occupant expressly objects. Do officers have any duty to locate and ask the other co-occupant before entering, or is it enough that he didn’t object at the threshold? How do Matlock, Randolph, and Fernandez apply when the nonconsenting occupant is present somewhere inside but not at the door, and the call involves domestic-violence allegations?

questions.title: What is the scope of consent during a welfare check, and why did officers still need a warrant afterward?
questions.question_body: The court says the wife’s consent allowed officers to enter to confirm the kids’ safety, scan the home, locate everyone, and ask basic questions—but they later got a warrant to search for guns. How do courts draw the objective-reasonableness line (Jimeno) between a consent-limited welfare check and a broader evidentiary search? In particular, does a welfare-check consent allow officers to open closed doors to locate people, conduct a Buie-style protective sweep without an arrest, or look in places where a person couldn’t be but a weapon could be? And if a firearm had been in plain view during the welfare check, could it have been seized without a warrant under plain view, or would that exceed the consent’s scope?

questions.title: Why did the Seventh Circuit review voluntariness and scope only for clear error despite relying on body-cam video?
questions.question_body: The opinion says voluntariness and scope are reviewed for clear error and then emphasizes that video can “evaporate any factual dispute.” Under Ornelas, probable cause and reasonable suspicion are reviewed de novo as mixed questions. Is voluntariness of consent (and scope) treated purely as factual in the Seventh Circuit, or as mixed questions elsewhere? When there’s body-cam video and no material factual dispute, do appellate courts ever treat the issue more like de novo because the facts are undisputed on the record?

questions.title: If the wife’s consent had been invalid, could exigent circumstances or inevitable discovery have saved the evidence?
questions.question_body: The panel didn’t reach the government’s exigency and inevitable-discovery arguments. Given the 911 report of threats to kill, kids inside, and the wife’s hesitation about their safety, would the emergency aid/exigent-circumstances doctrine (e.g., Brigham City v. Stuart; Michigan v. Fisher) have justified entry and a safety sweep regardless of consent, especially after Caniglia limited “community caretaking” in the home? Separately, could the firearms still be admissible under independent source or inevitable discovery (Nix; Murray) based on information available without the entry (e.g., the 911 call), or did the warrant application rely too heavily on statements obtained only after the entry (the children’s account)? What evidentiary showing does the government need in this posture?

questions.title: Could the wife validly consent to officers entering the husband’s separate bedroom under common or apparent authority?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that officers ultimately found the husband in a separate bedroom after a quick canvas. Under Matlock and Rodriguez, third-party consent requires common authority or, at least, apparent authority. Do courts generally treat a married spouse as having common or apparent authority to authorize entry into the other spouse’s separate bedroom (as opposed to truly private, exclusively controlled spaces)? In a welfare-check context, does the safety purpose expand the areas officers may enter (e.g., all rooms where a person could be), even if the consenting spouse might lack common authority over a particular room?

questions.title: How did Coleman preserve appellate review of the suppression ruling after pleading guilty?
questions.question_body: The defendant pled guilty but reserved the right to appeal the suppression denial. Am I right that this is a conditional plea under Fed. R. Crim. P. 11(a)(2)? What exactly must the parties and district court do to make that reservation effective (government consent, written specification of issues, etc.)? If he had entered an unconditional plea, would the suppression issue have been waived as a nonjurisdictional defect? Does the standard of review on appeal change in any way because of the conditional plea?

questions.title: Does the voluntariness inquiry consider a domestic-violence victim’s fear of the abuser, or only police coercion?
questions.question_body: The court focuses on the officer’s non-coercive tone and the lack of police pressure, and finds the wife’s consent voluntary. But in a domestic-violence scenario, could the victim’s fear of the abuser (rather than police) bear on whether consent is truly “free and voluntary”? Do courts limit the voluntariness analysis to state action (police coercion), or is a victim’s vulnerability, stress, or duress from a private actor also relevant under the totality of the circumstances?
